claims.text: Moving a transition-metal catalyst's d-band center closer to the Fermi level will increase catalytic activity in hydrogenation reactions.
Moving the d-band center closer to the Fermi level will increase hydrogenation selectivity.
The activity and selectivity improvements arise because the altered electronic structure optimizes adsorption energies of key intermediates.
Controlled alloying or strain can shift the d-band center closer to the Fermi level while preserving similar morphology.
The d-band-center position modulates surface electronic states.
The d-band-center position modulates adsorption energies of reactants and intermediates.
Shifting the d-band center closer to the Fermi level strengthens the binding of hydrogen and reaction intermediates up to an optimum.
Optimized binding facilitates a faster rate-determining hydrogenation step.
Adsorption that is too weak limits hydrogenation rates.
Adsorption that is too strong causes surface poisoning.
Balancing weak-adsorption and strong-adsorption limits improves both catalytic activity and selectivity.
Catalysts with the shifted d-band center will exhibit higher turnover frequencies than the unmodified catalyst.
Catalysts with the shifted d-band center will exhibit increased selectivity for the desired hydrogenated product relative to the unmodified catalyst.
The proposed relationship should hold under moderate hydrogenation conditions that do not cause sintering or phase changes.
XPS or UPS can be used to measure the d-band-center position.
Temperature-programmed desorption can provide adsorption-energy measurements.
A lack of statistically significant activity and selectivity improvement, or a lack of correlation with d-band-center shift, is designated as falsifying the hypothesis.

contradictions.description: The headline hypothesis and falsification rule treat movement closer to the Fermi level as directionally beneficial, whereas the mechanism states that benefit occurs only up to an optimum and that stronger binding can cause poisoning. Thus, a closer d-band center could reduce performance without necessarily refuting the proposed optimum-binding mechanism.
